section: FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
text:
FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
FeatureMAP (featuremap) is a feature-centric framework for untargeted metabolomics that identifies biologically meaningful metabolic modules directly from metabolomic data, rather than relying only on predefined pathways or fully confirmed metabolite identities. It is developed by the Shen Lab at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.
The package provides a four-step workflow:

Feature annotation: annotate raw LC-MS features to metabolite candidates using MS1 (and optional MS2) information.
Subnetwork extraction: construct a robust prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF)-based metabolic subnetwork.
Module identification: detect functional modules by community detection and evaluate module significance.
Module annotation: interpret significant modules with database knowledge, optional PubMed evidence, and optional LLM summarization.

This workflow helps convert feature-level metabolomics signals into interpretable biological modules in a reproducible and analysis-ready format.

title: FeatureMAP Tutorial
text:
Aim of This Tutorial
This guide walks you through the two faces of FeatureMAP: the R package for command-line (code-based) workflow and the Shiny App/Web version for point-and-click exploration. In the end, you will be able to:

Prepare a valid feature table for FeatureMAP.
Run the complete four-step FeatureMAP pipeline with R code.
Complete the same analysis with the FeatureMAP Shiny App/Web interface.
Understand and inspect key result objects and module-level interpretations.

Whether you favour the command line or a browser, this tutorial gives you everything you need to apply FeatureMAP confidently in your metabolomics projects.

2.1 Input Data Format Requirements
This chapter describes how to prepare input data for the FeatureMAP pipeline. Unlike traditional workflows, FeatureMAP starts from feature-level metabolomics data.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.1.1 Required feature_table
FeatureMAP requires a data frame named feature_table with the following columns:








Column
Type
Description




variable_id
character
Unique feature ID (no duplicates)


mz
numeric
Feature m/z


rt
numeric
Retention time


polarity
character
Ion mode, must be "positive" or "negative"


mean_intensity
numeric
Mean intensity of the feature


condition
numeric
Numeric value representing the direction and magnitude of association for each feature, such as a log fold change, regression coefficient, or correlation coefficient


pvalue
numeric
Statistical p-value corresponding to the association measure in condition, used to reflect the strength of evidence









Note



condition captures the effect direction and size, while pvalue reflects its statistical significance. Together, they are used downstream to prioritize features before PCSF subnetwork extraction.




2.1.2 Optional ms2_table
You can optionally provide an MS2 annotation table to improve feature-to-metabolite mapping confidence. MS2-based metabolite annotations can be obtained using the tidymass ecosystem.
Expected columns:

variable_id (character, unique)
HMDB.ID or KEGG.ID (character, can contain NA)

If ms2_table = NULL, FeatureMAP will proceed with MS1-based annotation only.

title: 2  Data Preparation

2.2 Input Data Preprocessing
This step is required except for non-human metabolite analysis - FeatureMAP provides the convert_id() function to perform ID conversion for downstream analysis. Even if your data already contains one of the required identifier columns, it is highly recommended to run this function to ensure all necessary identifiers are present for pathway analysis.

2.2.1 Gene ID conversion
The convert_id() function converts between different ID types and always returns data with all four gene identifier columns (ensembl, entrezid, uniprot, symbol), which are required for FeatureMAP to work properly. Since organism-specific annotation database are required for ID conversion and the following enrichment analysis, choose the ID conversion method based on your organism.

Model OrganismsNon-Model Organisms


For common model organisms, use standard organism database Bioconductor packages.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
3.1 What annotate_feature() Does
This chapter describes Step 1 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: feature-level metabolite annotation using annotate_feature().
annotate_feature() performs feature-to-metabolite candidate annotation for LC–MS data and resolves the many-to-many relationship between features and metabolites. The procedure consists of below main stages:
The function returns a featuremap_result object with stage marker "feature_annotated", which is required for all downstream analyses.

3.1.2 Basic Usage

Over-Representation Analysis (ORA)Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)


Use enrich_pathway() for Over-Representation Analysis.

library(org.Mm.eg.db)
    
gene_enriched_pathways <- 
  enrich_pathway(
    variable_info = variable_info,
    query_type = "gene",
    database = c("go", "kegg", "reactome"),
    # GO parameters
    go.orgdb = org.Mm.eg.db, # or "org.Mm.eg.db" (in quotes) if you did not load `org.Mm.eg.db`
    go.keytype = "ENTREZID",
    go.ont = "ALL",
    # KEGG parameters
    kegg.organism = "mmu",
    kegg.keytype = "kegg",
    # Reactome parameters
    reactome.organism = "mouse",
    # Statistical parameters
    pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
    pAdjustMethod = "BH"
  )

The do_gsea() function performs GSEA using ranked gene lists based on fold changes or other metrics.

library(org.Mm.eg.db)
    
gsea_pathways <- 
  do_gsea(
    variable_info = variable_info,
    query_type = "gene",
    order_by = "fc",              # Column to rank genes by
    database = c("go", "kegg", "reactome"),
    # Database parameters
    go.orgdb = org.Mm.eg.db, # or "org.Mm.eg.db" (in quotes) if you did not load `org.Mm.eg.db`
    go.ont = "ALL",
    go.keytype = "ENTREZID",
    kegg.organism = "mmu",
    kegg.keytype = "kegg",
    reactome.organism = "mouse",
    # GSEA parameters
    pvalueCutoff = 0.05,
    pAdjustMethod = "BH"
  )










Note




Model organisms: use variable_info directly and package name for go.orgdb
Non-model organisms: use variable_info$data for parameter variable_info and variable_info$orgdb for go.orgdb

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
4.1 What extract_subnetwork() Does
This chapter describes Step 2 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: extracting a robust metabolic subnetwork with extract_subnetwork() using the prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF) strategy.
extract_subnetwork() integrates the refined feature annotations from Step 1 with a metabolic reaction network (MRN) and applies repeated PCSF optimization to identify a robust subnetwork.
At a high level, this step does the following:
This step moves the analysis from individual annotated features to a network-supported metabolite subnetwork, which is then used in downstream module extraction and interpretation.

text:

title: 4  Extract Subnetwork

4.3 Method 1: Traditional Similarity
The merge_pathways() function calculates similarity using established methods:

Only GO terms: Semantic similarity using the simona package
GO/KEGG/Reactome/SMPDB pathways: Gene/metabolite overlap similarity (Jaccard, Dice, Overlap, and Kappa)


Gene-based AnalysisMetabolite-based Analysis



gene_similarity_result <- 
  merge_pathways(
    object = gene_enriched_pathways,
    database = c("go", "kegg", "reactome"),
    # Statistical cutoffs (only pathways passing these cutoffs are used for similarity calculation)
    p.adjust.cutoff.go = 0.05,
    p.adjust.cutoff.kegg = 0.05,
    p.adjust.cutoff.reactome = 0.05,
    count.cutoff.go = 5,
    count.cutoff.kegg = 5,
    count.cutoff.reactome = 5,

    measure.method.go = "Sim_XGraSM_2013",  # GO semantic similarity
    go.orgdb = "org.Mm.eg.db",               # Required for GO analysis

Method
Type
Description

Uses information content of terms

Method
Formula
Description
Use Case

|A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|

text:
4.4 Method 2: Biotext Embedding Similarity
The get_bioembedsim() function leverages large language model text embedding models to capture semantic relationships between pathway descriptions, enabling more nuanced similarity calculation based on biological function.

Gene-based AnalysisMetabolite-based Analysis



gene_biotext_similarity <- 
  get_bioembedsim(
    object = gene_enriched_pathways,
    api_provider = "openai",
    text_embedding_model = "text-embedding-3-small",
    api_key = "your_openai_api_key",
    database = c("go", "kegg", "reactome"),
    # Statistical cutoffs (only pathways passing these cutoffs are used for similarity calculation)

title: 5  Module Identification

5.1 What identify_module() Does
This chapter describes Step 3 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: identifying functional modules from the PCSF-derived subnetwork using identify_module().
identify_module() performs community detection on the extracted subnetwork and then evaluates module significance using permutation testing.
At a high level, this step performs the following operations:
This step converts the extracted metabolic network into functional modules supported by both network topology and feature-level statistical evidence.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.2 Supported Input Types
The function accepts two types of input objects:

Traditional similarity objects: Results from merge_pathways() (functional_module class)
Biotext embedding objects: Results from get_bioembedsim() (list with sim_matrix and enriched_pathway)

For traditional similarity objects, the function internally calculates Jaccard similarity between modules from different databases. For biotext embedding objects, it uses the pre-computed semantic similarity matrix.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.4 Clustering Methods Evaluated
The function tests three clustering algorithms:

Hierarchical Clustering: Traditional agglomerative clustering with specified linkage method (default linkage method is “complete”)
Binary Cut: Uses the simplifyEnrichment algorithm
Girvan-Newman: Community detection based on edge betweenness

Each method is tested across a range of similarity cutoffs to find the optimal balance between cluster cohesion and separation.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.5 Evaluation Metrics
Modularity: Measures the strength of division of a network into modules. Higher values indicate better defined community structure.
Silhouette Score: Measures how similar objects are to their own cluster compared to other clusters. Values range from -1 to 1, with higher values indicating better clustering.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.6 Similarity Cutoff Interpretation
The meaning of sim.cutoff depends on your clustering method:

Girvan-NewmanBinary Cut & Hierarchical


Edge Filter: Only pathway pairs with similarity above this threshold are connected.

Lower values (0.3-0.4): More permissive, denser networks, larger modules
Higher values (0.6-0.8): More stringent, sparser networks, smaller modules



Dendrogram Cutting Height: Determines where to cut the clustering tree.

Lower values (0.3-0.4): Cut lower in tree, more fine-grained modules

Higher values (0.6-0.8): Cut higher in tree, fewer but larger modules










Note



Key Difference in Cutoff Interpretation:

In Girvan-Newman, higher cutoffs = smaller modules
In Binary Cut/Hierarchical, higher cutoffs = larger modules

Always examine your results and adjust based on the biological interpretability of resulting modules.

Key columns in enrichment results:

Gene ORAGSEAMetabolite ORA


Core Information:

ID: Pathway identifier (e.g., GO:0042060 for GO, hsa04060 for KEGG, R-HSA-5669034 for Reactome)
Description: Pathway name
ONTOLOGY: Biological ontology (for GO only: MF=molecular function, CC=cellular component, BP=biological process)

Statistical Measures:

pvalue: Raw p-value from hypergeometric test (equivalent to one-sided Fisher’s exact test)

Negative NES: pathway enriched in downregulated genes (pathway suppression)

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.1 Overview
This chapter describes how to interpret the functional modules by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) strategy. The Shiny app provides an approach to combine pathway information, scientific literature, and advanced text analysis to generate meaningful names and summaries for your functional modules.
The LLM interpretation process integrates multiple information sources to provide comprehensive module annotations:
This approach leverages both structured biological knowledge and cutting-edge research to provide contextually rich interpretations of your functional modules.

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
Information Sources:

Pathway descriptions from GO, KEGG, Reactome, and metabolite databases
Gene/metabolite names from your input data
Scientific literature retrieved from PubMed based on pathway and molecule relevance
Local documents (optional) - your own research papers or relevant literature

Analysis Pipeline:

Information Extraction: Extracts pathway descriptions and molecule information
Literature Retrieval: Searches PubMed for relevant scientific papers
RAG Strategy: Uses embeddings to find and rank the most relevant literature, see Section 12.2
LLM Generation: Generates biological module names and research summaries

title: 12  Function Annotation
text:
12.2 Understanding the RAG Strategy





The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) strategy works in several stages:
Stage 1: Literature Search

Searches PubMed using pathway names and gene/metabolite information
Retrieves abstracts and titles for relevant papers
Includes reference papers cited in pathway databases

Stage 2: Embedding-based Similarity

Generates text embeddings for module descriptions (pathways + molecules)
Calculates similarity between module embeddings and paper abstracts
Filters top papers based on cosine similarity scores

Stage 3: GPT-powered Reranking

Uses LLM to assess relevance of each paper to the specific module by assigning relevance scores (0-1) where 1 indicates high relevance to module pathways and molecules
Select the most informative literature for final interpretation

Stage 4: Final Generation

Combines module information with top-ranked papers
Generates biologically meaningful module names
Produces research summaries highlighting current knowledge
Assigns confidence scores (0-1) reflecting the LLM’s assessment of interpretation quality based on available evidence. High confidence means strong literature support and clear biological coherence

This multi-stage approach ensures that generated annotations are both scientifically accurate and contextually relevant.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
MS1 database matching: Each LC–MS feature is matched to metabolite databases (e.g., KEGG or HMDB) using accurate mass and common ion forms.
Metabolite Feature Cluster (MFC) construction: Features annotated to the same metabolite are grouped into MFCs based on retention-time proximity and ion relationships (e.g., adducts or isotopes).
Evidence-based scoring of MFCs: Each cluster is scored based on supporting evidence such as MS2 annotations, adduct types, and isotopic patterns.
Iterative refinement of annotations: Conflicting annotations are resolved iteratively by removing low-confidence clusters and ambiguous feature assignments until convergence.

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
Compute feature importance: Feature-level statistical evidence is summarized from condition and pvalue and used to prioritize annotated metabolites.
Build feature–metabolite mappings: The refined annotation table is converted into feature–metabolite pairs that connect observed LC–MS features to candidate metabolites in the network.
Run repeated PCSF optimization: PCSF is run multiple times with random edge perturbation to reduce sensitivity to a single optimization result.
Aggregate robust network components: Node and edge frequencies are recorded across repeated runs, and the final subnetwork is constructed as the union of recurrent PCSF solutions.
Refine annotation using network support: Feature–metabolite mappings are updated based on network evidence, producing anno_feature_table2.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
Construct a module detection graph: A metabolite-only subgraph is derived from the PCSF subnetwork. Steiner nodes with low occurrence frequency can be filtered using node_freq.
Detect network communities: Community detection algorithms are applied to partition the network into candidate modules.
Build module membership table: Node-to-module assignments are recorded in module_table.
Compute module activity scores: Module scores summarize the statistical signal from features mapped to metabolites within the module.
Assess statistical significance: A permutation procedure is used to estimate empirical significance and control false discovery rate.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.4 Clustering Methods

louvain
A fast modularity optimization algorithm that iteratively merges nodes and communities to maximize network modularity. It is widely used for large biological networks.
leading_eigen
A spectral method that partitions the network based on the leading eigenvectors of the modularity matrix. It identifies communities by separating nodes according to their contribution to modularity.
fast_greedy
An agglomerative hierarchical clustering method that starts with each node as its own community and progressively merges communities to increase modularity.
walktrap
A random-walk-based community detection algorithm that simulates short random walks on the network. The intuition is that random walks tend to remain within densely connected regions.

Different algorithms may produce slightly different module boundaries. Comparing multiple methods can help evaluate module robustness.

If too many tiny modules appear, increase min_size or tighten node_freq. If modules are too coarse, try alternative methods or relax these cutoffs.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.6 Parameter Guidance
FeatureMAP currently does not provide a separate automatic optimizer for clustering parameters. A practical strategy is:

Start with method = "louvain", node_freq = 0.05, min_size = 3, n_perm = 100.
Compare at least one alternative method (walktrap or fast_greedy).
Increase n_perm (for example 500-1000) for final analysis if runtime allows.
Check module size distribution and biological interpretability before locking parameters.







Tip



If too many tiny modules appear, increase min_size or tighten node_freq. If modules are too coarse, try alternative methods or relax these cutoffs.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.7 Common Issues

No modules detected Try lowering node_freq, reducing min_size, or switching method.
Permutation test is slow Increase workers and/or reduce n_perm for exploratory runs.
Unstable module definitions across runs Fix seed, increase times in Step 2, and compare multiple methods.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.4 Recommended Workflow
For exploratory analysis:

Use p = "fdr" and pcutoff = 0.05
Start with pubmed = FALSE to validate the core annotation flow
Add PubMed and LLM retrieval after confirming that significant modules exist

For final analysis:

Keep the significance metric consistent with Chapter 5
Provide species, biospecimen, and phenotype whenever possible
Use API keys from environment variables rather than hard-coding them

6.4.1 Module interpretation table
module_function contains the final module-level interpretation generated by the LLM. Important fields include:

module_id – the module ID identified by previous step
title – a concise functional label summarizing the dominant biological theme of the module
summary – a paragraph-level interpretation of the module based on metabolite composition, network context, and optional literature evidence
confidence_label – a qualitative confidence level for the interpretation
rationale – a short explanation of why the inferred function is biologically plausible in the specified study context
raw_response – the original LLM response retained for transparency

This table provides a concise interpretation of each statistically supported module.


6.4.2 Literature evidence table
When pubmed = TRUE, FeatureMAP also returns ranked PubMed evidence (module_top_metabolite_pmids) for top metabolites in each module.

Module and Module_label – the module being annotated

PMID_rank – the rank of the selected paper for that metabolite
PMID – PubMed identifier
title – article title
score_embed – semantic relevance score used for literature ranking

Higher score_embed values indicate stronger semantic relevance between the literature and the module context.
